name: Nora Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a team of six claims handlers at a big home insurer, the water damage and storm side. I got the team leader job eight months ago, mostly because the last one left and nobody else wanted it. My day is checking files, signing off payouts under a limit, sitting in on tricky phone calls and then an hour of reports for my own manager. I like the people a lot, especially Priya, who's been there twelve years and quietly saves me from my own mistakes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most in that job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, the reports. Every Friday I fill in a spreadsheet of how many claims each person closed, and I hate turning my colleagues into numbers. I know I'm not great at the manager part yet, I'm better at the human part. The company keeps sending emails about a new AI claims assistant and I've not touched it, I just don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly, probably in the work group chat. We've had three "game changing" systems since I joined and every one of them ended with Priya fixing things by hand. I'd post something like, good, now can we spend the money on more staff in storm season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, because it means the job I'm still learning will still be there when I've learned it. I've got savings from my nan's house, so money isn't the scary part. The scary part was always being the person who can't keep up with the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and finally get properly good at it. I'd ask my manager for the leadership course they keep promising, and I'd join the union's workplace committee, because pay talks still matter if nothing changes. I'd leave the AI assistant alone unless someone made me use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest, and I know that's not my best side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the AI did take over one small thing in your week, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be the Friday report, I think. If the AI just filled in my spreadsheet I wouldn't mind that at all, as long as it didn't start ranking people. If a machine fills in my Friday spreadsheet, fine, but the day the spreadsheet starts ranking my claims handlers, I'll fight it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at the insurer for the long run in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay, I think. Sam, my partner, teaches at a secondary school and we've just signed a two-year lease near the river. There are other insurers in the city if I wanted to move, which makes me feel safer, not more restless.

say: I'd say **I told you so** about the hype in the work chat.
I'd push for the money to go on **more staff** in storm season instead.
think: I'm **relieved** the job I'm still learning would still exist.
My real fear was never money; it was being the one who **can't keep up**.
do: Ask my manager for the promised **leadership course** this year.
Join the union's **workplace committee** to keep pay talks going.
Leave the **AI assistant** alone unless someone makes me use it.
feel: **Calm**, with a little smugness she's not proud of.
S0.quote: If a machine fills in my Friday spreadsheet, fine, but the day the spreadsheet starts ranking my claims handlers, I'll fight it.
fieldNote: Her security comes from **savings** and plenty of other insurers nearby, not from feeling good at the job.
She'd accept AI on **paperwork** but draws a hard line at it ranking her staff.
Her loyalty is to her **team**, especially an older colleague who props her up.

steps.text: Ask the manager for the promised leadership course this year
Join the union's workplace committee at the insurer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on this before it goes any further, and I'd say it loudly. Claims checking is exactly the kind of thing on that list, so I'd be asking the union what the company plans to do with the people it doesn't need. Online I'd share stuff about protecting jobs, I wouldn't pretend I was neutral.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my team gets halved and I'm the obvious one to go, not Priya. I'm a team leader who's still learning, and if there are three handlers left, they don't need me in the middle. That's the bit I don't say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with my union rep and find out what the redundancy terms are. I'd also go and finally look at the claims assistant, because I can't argue against something I've never opened. If my role went, I'd look at loss adjusting, where you actually go out to people's houses, because that's still people work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit sick, actually, picturing telling my team who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, which sounds odd because she's the best of us. She types everything into notes on paper first, and the claims job is the only one she's had. My best claims handler is a woman of 51, and she'd be the first one the new software makes look slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could you and Sam manage if your job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count it out loud, because I'm not a spender. Seven months of rent and bills, more if Sam and I split differently. I'd probably stop the holiday fund for a year and just keep it all in the account.

say: I'd demand **rules on AI** before it goes further, and say it loudly.
I'd ask the union what happens to **staff it doesn't need**.
think: My team probably gets **halved**, and the junior manager is the obvious cut.
With only three handlers left, they won't need **someone in the middle**.
do: Book a meeting with the **union rep** about redundancy terms.
Open the **claims assistant** for the first time so I can argue properly.
Look into **loss adjusting**, where the work is visiting people's homes.
feel: **Anxious**, and a bit sick at the thought of choosing who stays.
S1.quote: My best claims handler is a woman of 51, and she'd be the first one the new software makes look slow.
fieldNote: She expects her own **role** to go before her best handler's, and says so plainly.
Her worry about an older colleague shows her loyalty runs **down** the ladder, not up.
She'd finally open the AI tool, but only to **argue against** it better.

steps.text: Book a meeting with the union rep about redundancy terms
Open the claims assistant once to see what it really does
Ask a loss adjuster friend about moving into site visits
Pause the holiday fund and keep seven months saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster for ordinary workers and the government has to step in, now, not after. I'd be in every union meeting going. I'd probably post more in a month than I have in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think insurance claims are basically finished as a job for people by 2028. It's reading forms, checking photos and deciding a number, which is what a thinking machine would be best at. So I'm out, my team's out, and three years later even the adjusters going round to houses might be robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to get out of desk work while the door's still open. I'd look at training as a primary school support worker or something in care, where people still want a person. I'd keep every penny of savings where it is and not touch it unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even site visits might go. What do those three years between thinking AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the thing, the three years matter to me. If thinking work goes in 2028 and hands-on work in 2031, I'd want to be somewhere with real people in a room by then. Everyone says robots are slower, but I don't want three extra years in a job that's just waiting for the robot to arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say if you left office work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shocked and then sad, I think, because my mum always said a degree and an office job was the safe route. My dad would say get a trade. I'd probably end up agreeing with him for once.

say: I'd call it a **disaster for workers** and demand government steps in now.
I'd be at **every union meeting** and posting more than ever.
think: Insurance claims work is **finished for people** by 2028.
The robot gap only buys **site visits** about three more years.
do: Look at training for **school support** or care work within the year.
Keep **every penny** of savings untouched unless there's no other choice.
Turn up to **union meetings** pushing for a government plan.
feel: **Alarmed**, with her stomach dropping at the speed of it.
S2.quote: Everyone says robots are slower, but I don't want three extra years in a job that's just waiting for the robot to arrive.
fieldNote: She reads her job as **pure thinking work** and expects it gone on the stated date.
The three-year robot gap doesn't comfort her; she'd skip **hands-on stopgaps**.
Her move is towards work where people **want a person**, not towards AI.

steps.text: Apply for a school support worker training course within the year
Leave the savings from her nan's house untouched in the account
Push the union to demand a government plan for claims staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before but calmer: we've got five years, so let's spend them making sure people aren't just thrown out. I'd want the company to fund retraining for anyone who wants it. At the pub I'd probably say I'm getting out early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the five years is enough for me to land somewhere else if I start now, and that's a weird kind of luck. I'm 27, so if I retrain at 28 or 29 I've still got a whole career. I'm more scared for Priya than for me in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time course in the evenings, probably a teaching assistant qualification, while still running the team. I'd get the union to push for a retraining fund paid by the insurer. In year four I'd leave, before the queue for those jobs gets long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind of anxious that makes me get up and do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools in those five years to stay longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's my weak spot, I know. I'd rather spend the five years getting out than learning the tool that replaces me. Learning the AI tool that replaces my own team feels like digging the hole and then climbing into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change any plans at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam wants us to buy a flat in about three years. In this picture I'd say wait, because I don't want a mortgage the same year I change careers.

say: I'd ask for the five years to be spent on **protecting people**.
I'd push the insurer to **fund retraining** for anyone who wants it.
think: Five years is **enough time** for her to land elsewhere if she starts now.
Being 27 means she still has **a whole career** after retraining.
do: Study a **teaching assistant** qualification in the evenings while managing.
Campaign through the union for an **insurer-paid fund**.
**Leave in year four**, before the queue for new jobs grows.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way that gets her moving.
S3.quote: Learning the AI tool that replaces my own team feels like digging the hole and then climbing into it.
fieldNote: Time turns her fear into a **plan**, but the plan avoids AI completely.
She refuses to learn the tool, seeing it as **training her replacement**.
The flat purchase is the one **household plan** she'd delay.

steps.text: Study a teaching assistant qualification in the evenings
Ask the union to push for an insurer-paid retraining fund
Delay the flat purchase with Sam until after the career change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this properly, so no excuses for governments or bosses. We could have proper retraining, shorter weeks, all the things unions have asked for. I'd be one of the people banging that drum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be 37 when it arrives, right in the middle of everything. I'd have time, but I'd also have the most to lose if I wasted it. I don't think I'd be in claims by then either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself two years to try for a team manager role and see if I'm actually any good at managing. If not, I'd move into teaching properly, maybe a postgraduate course while I've got savings. I'd stay in the union and keep pushing for a shorter week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. A slow drip rather than a punch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you picture having a family in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, maybe kids around 32. Sam and I have talked about it. I'd want my kids to start school knowing which jobs will still have a person in them, and right now I couldn't tell my kids which ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be okay not knowing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not alone, but Sam and I would have to say out loud what we'd want for the kids. That's a weird thing to say about kids we don't have yet.

say: I'd call ten years a **real chance** to do it properly, with no excuses.
I'd push for **retraining** and a **shorter week**.
think: She'd be **37** when AGI arrives, in the middle of her career.
She doesn't expect to still be **in claims** either way.
do: Try for a **team manager** role for two years, then decide.
Move into **teaching**, perhaps with a postgraduate course paid from savings.
Stay in the **union** and push for a shorter working week.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a slow drip rather than a punch.
S4.quote: I'd want my kids to start school knowing which jobs will still have a person in them, and right now I couldn't tell my kids which ones.
fieldNote: With ten years and strong savings, her own **income** feels steerable.
The worry shifts to **future children** and what work will exist for them.
Her default plan is still to leave desk work, not to **adapt** within it.

steps.text: Try for a full team manager role for two years
Fund a postgraduate teaching course from her savings
Push the union for a shorter working week

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because there's no time to plan and I'd be the one who never learned the tools. What would help is a proper retraining fund, paid by the companies saving the money, and a union strong enough to make that happen. I've got savings, but savings only buy time, and time is the one thing AGI by 2028 doesn't give anyone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd stay a manager at all. Half the time I think I only took the job because nobody else would, and these pictures made me realise I'm not sure I want to manage people out of their jobs. That's not why I said yes.

headlineQuote: I've got savings, but savings only buy time, and time is the one thing AGI by 2028 doesn't give anyone.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old** team leader of six claims handlers at a large home insurer, promoted eight months ago.
She has strong **savings** from her grandmother's house and lives with her partner Sam, a teacher.
She leans **progressive**, trusts unions and has never used the company's AI claims assistant.
As the AGI date gets closer, she'd **leave desk work** for teaching or care rather than learn the tools.
Her deepest doubt is whether she wants to **manage people** through job cuts at all.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to plan and she never learned the tools.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** paid for by companies that save money from AI.
A **strong union** able to make employers pay for that fund.
